lesson.title: Grounded Without a Wire: The Virtual Ground Node
lesson.summary: A virtual ground is the special case of the virtual short that arises when the non-inverting input of an op-amp is tied to real ground, causing the inverting input to sit at approximately zero volts as well, even though nothing wires it directly to ground.
lesson.body:
Many of the most common op-amp circuits, including the inverting amplifier taken up in the next chapter, connect the non-inverting input, V+, directly to real, physical ground, so that V+ = 0 volts exactly. Combine this with the virtual short from the previous chapter, which established that V- follows V+ under negative feedback, and the conclusion is immediate: V- also sits at approximately 0 volts. This node, V-, is called a virtual ground.

The word virtual is doing real work in that name, and the distinction from an actual electrical ground connection matters. A real ground is a fixed, actively maintained 0 volt reference, generally the return path of the power supply, capable of sourcing or sinking as much current as the wiring and supply can handle. A virtual ground, by contrast, holds at 0 volts only because negative feedback is continuously and dynamically adjusting the op-amp's output to keep V- equal to V+. It is a moving target that happens to always land on zero, not a fixed rail.

This distinction has a sharp practical consequence: if the feedback path is ever broken, for example if a feedback resistor is desoldered or a feedback trace opens, the virtual ground disappears instantly. Nothing is left to pin V- at zero, so it floats freely, and the op-amp, no longer restrained by feedback, drives its output to whatever supply rail the resulting large open-loop gain pushes it toward, exactly the saturated behavior described back in the open-loop gain chapter. A real ground would never behave this way, it stays at zero regardless of what else happens in the circuit.

The reason the virtual ground concept earns its own chapter, rather than being treated as a footnote to the virtual short, is how useful it is for analysis. Because V- is pinned at 0 volts, any resistor connecting an input voltage to that node has the full input voltage across it, letting a designer compute the current through that resistor with plain Ohm's law, current equals the input voltage divided by the resistor, without needing to think about the op-amp's internal behavior at all. That current, combined with the infinite input impedance assumption (no current can escape into the op-amp itself), is precisely the tool used to derive the inverting amplifier's gain in the next chapter.
